• equal-sharing context showing that one half and two fourths are equal:
    • 6 pieces of string are to be shared by 4 students to make bracelets. How many pieces of string does each student get?
      • In this situation, students are supported in recognizing that for both solutions, the students will get the same amount of string, that is, 1 and one half is the same as 1 and 2 one fourths, or 1 and two fourths.

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• When something is shared fairly, or equally as two pieces, each piece is 1 one half of the original amount. Two one halves make up a whole.
  • When something is shared fairly, or equally as four pieces, each piece is 1 one fourth of the original amount. Four one fourths make up a whole.
  • If the original amount is shared as two pieces or four pieces, the fractions one half and two fourths are equivalent.
  • A half of a half is a fourth.
  • If something is cut in half, it is not possible for one person to get “the big half” while the other person gets “the small half”. If something is cut in half, both pieces are exactly equal. If there is a “big half”, then it isn’t a half.

Note

  • Words can have multiple meanings. It is important to be aware that in many situations, fair does not mean equal, and equal is not equitable. Educators should clarify how they are using the term “fair share” and ensure that students understand that in the math context fair means equal and the intent behind such math problems is to find equal amounts.
  • Different fractions can describe the same amount as long as they are based on the same whole.
  • The size of the whole matters. If 1 one half and 1 one fourth are based on the same whole, then 1 one half is twice as big as 1 one fourth. But if a small sticky note is cut into halves, and a big piece of chart paper is cut into fourths, then the 1 one fourth of the chart paper is bigger than the 1 one half of the sticky note.
  • The fair-share problems that students engage in for learning around B1.6 will provide the opportunity to notice that 1 one half and 2 one fourths are the same amount.
  • Students in this grade are not expected to write fractions symbolically; they should write “half”, not “$$\frac{1}{2}$$”.

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
Create and pose equal-sharing situations with 4 sharers, where students can arrive at equivalent answers (e.g., by using one half or two fourths). For example:

  • 10 carrot sticks are to be shared by 4 friends. How many carrot sticks does each friend get?
  • 4 Elders want to share 6 pieces of bannock. How many pieces of bannock does each Elder get?

Encourage students to act out the situation using pieces of paper, or model it with a simple drawing, and use the language of mixed numbers and fractions (e.g., 1 and one half, 1 and two fourths) to describe the result. As students share their solutions, have them determine whether answers with one half and those with two fourths represent the same amount. Support the conversation by having them use their drawings and models to explain their thinking.

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• When one whole is shared equally by a number of sharers, the number of sharers determines the size of each individual portion and is reflected in how that portion is named. For example, if a whole is equally shared among eight people, the whole has been split into eighths, and each part is one eighth of the whole. One eighth is a unit fraction, and there are 8 one eighths in a whole.
  • The size of the whole matters. When comparing fractions as numbers, it is assumed they refer to the same-sized whole. Without a common whole, it is quite possible for one fourth to be larger than one half.
  • Sharing a whole equally among more sharers creates smaller shares; conversely, sharing a whole equally among fewer sharers creates larger shares. So, for example, 1 one fourth is larger than 1 one fifth, when taken from the same whole or set.

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
Have students compare the results of sharing the same amount with different numbers of sharers and use these experiences to compare and order unit fractions. The following are examples of this type of equal-sharing situation:

  • Who gets more melon, the friend equally sharing a melon with seven other friends or the friend equally sharing the same-size melon with eight other friends?
  • The baker at Sweet Treats Bakery has just made two desserts in two different but identical rectangular pans. The baker cuts the tres leches cake in one pan into six equal-size pieces and the baklava in the other pan into eight equal-size pieces. Which pieces are bigger, the cake or the baklava? How do you know?
  • The teacher has two sheets of construction paper that are exactly the same size and is preparing for a craft activity to make pinwheels. The teacher cuts the blue sheet of construction paper into four equal-size pieces and the red sheet into six equal-size pieces. Each pinwheel uses one of the pieces cut from the blue construction paper and one of the pieces cut from the red construction paper. Is the pinwheel more blue or more red? How do you know?

Support students in using the language of unit fractions (e.g., one sixth, one eighth, one fourth) to describe the size of each portion. Have them order the unit fractions from largest to smallest. Draw out the idea that more shares means smaller pieces and emphasize that this idea is helpful in understanding and comparing fractions.

    • facts with zero:

        • 7 – 0 = 7:
    • doubles facts:
        • 4 + 4 = 8:
          • can be linked to mnemonic devices; for example, “double 4 is a spider with 4 legs on one side and 4 legs on the other”:
    • “near-doubles” or “doubles-plus-one” facts:

    • “make 10” facts:

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• Understanding the relationships that exist among numbers and among operations provides strategies for learning basic facts.
  • Knowing the fact families can help with recalling the math facts (e.g., 4 + 6 = 10, 10 – 4 = 6, and 10 – 6 = 4).
  • There are many strategies that can help with developing and understanding the math facts:
    • Counting on and counting back supports + 1, + 2, − 1, and − 2 facts.
    • The commutative property (e.g., 6 + 4 = 10 and 4 + 6 = 10).
    • The identity property (e.g., 6 + 0 = 6 and 6 – 0 = 6).
    • Doubles, doubles + 1, and doubles – 1 (e.g., 4 + 5 can be thought of as 4 + 4 plus 1 more; 9 can be thought of as 10 less 1 or double 5 less one).

Note

  • Addition and subtraction are inverse operations. This means that addition facts can be used to understand and recall subtraction facts (e.g., 5 + 3 = 8, so 8 – 5 = 3 and 8 – 3 = 5).
  • Having automatic recall of addition and subtraction facts is useful when carrying out mental and written calculations and frees up working memory when solving complex problems and tasks.

        • 20 – 17:
          • start at 17 and count up by 1s: “18, 19, 20” (3 is the result)
    • counting back by ones:

          • start at 13 and count down by 1s to 11: “12, 11” (2 is the result)
    • subtracting in parts:
        • 16 – 7:
            • first, evaluate 16 − 6 = 10
            • then, subtract 1 more to get 9
    • using compensation:

          • change to 19 − 9 (add 1 to 18)

• Mental math refers to doing calculations in one’s head. Sometimes the numbers or the number of steps in a calculation are too complex to completely hold in one’s head, so jotting down partial calculations and diagrams can be used to complete the calculations.
  • Estimation is a useful mental strategy when either an exact answer is not needed or there is insufficient time to work out a calculation.

Note

  • To do calculations in one’s head involves using flexible strategies that build on known facts, number relationships, and counting strategies. These strategies continue to expand and develop through the grades.
  • Mental math may or may not be quicker than paper-and-pencil strategies, but speed is not the goal. The value of mental math is in its portability and flexibility, since it does not require a calculator or paper and pencil. Practising mental math strategies also deepens an understanding of the relationships between numbers.
  • Estimation can be used to check the reasonableness of calculations and should be continually encouraged when students are doing mathematics.
  • Number lines, circular number lines, and part-whole models can help students visualize and communicate mental math strategies.

elaboration.value:
• Situations involving addition and subtraction may involve:
    • adding a quantity onto an existing amount or removing a quantity from an existing amount;
    • combining two or more quantities;
    • comparing quantities.
  • Acting out a situation by representing it with objects, a drawing, or a diagram can support students in identifying the given quantities in a problem and the unknown quantity.
  • Set models can be used to add a quantity on to an existing amount or to remove a quantity from an existing amount.
  • Linear models can be used to determine the difference between two numbers by comparing quantities.
  • Part-whole models can be used to show the relationship between what is known and what is unknown and how addition and subtraction relate to the situation.

Note

  • An important part of problem solving is the ability to choose the operation that matches the action in a situation. Addition and subtraction are useful for showing:
    • when a quantity changes, either by joining another quantity to it or separating a quantity from it;
    • when two quantities (parts) are combined to make one whole quantity;
    • when two quantities are compared.
  • In addition and subtraction, what is unknown can vary:
    • In change situations, sometimes the result is unknown, sometimes the starting point is unknown, and sometimes the change is unknown.
    • In combine situations, sometimes one part is unknown, sometimes the other part is unknown, and sometimes the total is unknown.
    • In compare situations, sometimes the larger number is unknown, sometimes the smaller number is unknown, and sometimes the difference is unknown.
  • It is important to model the corresponding equation that represents the situation. The unknown may appear anywhere in an equation (e.g., 8 + ? = 19; ? + 11 = 19; or 8 + 11 = ?), and matching the structure of the equation to what is happening in the situation reinforces the meaning of addition and subtraction.
  • Sometimes changing a “non-standard” equation (where the unknown is not after the equal sign) into its “standard form” can make it easier to carry out the calculation. Part-whole models make the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction evident and help students develop a flexible understanding of the equal sign. These are important ideas in the development of algebraic reasoning.
  • Counting up or counting down are strategies students may use to determine an unknown quantity.

Note

• Different representations are used for different purposes to convey different types of information. Tally tables, concrete graphs, and pictographs are used to represent counts or frequencies of various categories.
  • Information in tally tables, concrete graphs, and pictographs can prompt the asking and answering of questions like "Which category has the greatest frequency?".
  • Sometimes, considering the frequency can support making informed decisions, such as what type of books should be ordered for the class library.
  • Questions of interest are intended to be answered through the analysis of the representations. Sometimes the analysis raises more questions that require further collection, representation, and analysis of data.

Note

  • There are three levels of graph comprehension that students should learn about and practise:
    • Level 1: information is read directly from the graph and no interpretation is required.
    • Level 2: information is read and used to compare (e.g., greatest, least) or perform operations (e.g., addition, subtraction).
    • Level 3: information is read and used to make inferences about the data using background knowledge of the topic.
  • Analysing data can be complex, so it is important to provide students with strategies that will support them to build these skills.

Ask students to rearrange the data in a concrete graph so that the categories are in order from greatest (highest) frequency to least (lowest) frequency.

Next, give students the same information in a pictograph. Ask them which category has the greatest (highest) frequency and to describe how they know – for example, “kiwi” on the pictograph has the greatest frequency because it has the longest line. Similarly, ask them which category has the lowest frequency and how they know.

Finally, give students the same information in a tally chart. Ask them which category has the greatest (highest) frequency and to describe how they know – for example, “kiwi” on the tally chart has the greatest frequency because it has a group of five like the apple category, and one more. Similarly, ask them which category has the lowest frequency and how they know.

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• Geometric shapes exist in two dimensions (pictures or drawings) and in three dimensions (objects).
  • Three-dimensional objects and two-dimensional shapes can be sorted by identifying and paying attention to similarities and ignoring differences.
  • Shapes and objects have more than one, and often many, attributes, so they can be sorted in more than one way. Sorting rules indicate which attribute to sort for and are used to determine what belongs and what does not belong in a group.
  • Attributes are characteristics or features of an object or shape (e.g., length, area, colour, texture, ability to roll). Attributes can be used to describe, compare, sort, and measure.
  • Geometric properties are specific attributes that are the same for an entire “class” of shapes or objects. So, for example, a group of shapes might all be red (attribute), but in order for them all to be squares, they must have four equal sides and four right angles (the geometric properties of a square). Geometric properties are used to identify two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects.

Note

  • Sorting by attributes is used in counting, measurement, and geometry. When a student counts “this” and not “that”, they have sorted; when they measure length, they focus on one attribute and not another; when they say that this shape is a triangle and not a square, their sorting has led them to identify the shape.

content.value: describe the relative locations of objects or people, using positional language

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• Positional language often includes direction and distance to describe the location of one object in relation to another.
  • Words and phrases such as above, below, to the left, to the right, behind, and in front describe the position of one object in relation to another. Numbers can describe the distance of one object from another.

content.name: Content
content.value: give and follow directions for moving from one location to another

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• directional language:
    • right/left; e.g., the frog moves two hops to the right
    • forward/backward
    • up/down
  • contexts:
    • movements to locate an object
    • movements of a character on a grid

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• Movement encompasses distance and direction.
  • Words or phrases such as above, below, to the left, to the right, behind, or in front of describe the direction of one object in relation to another. Numbers can describe the distance of one object from another.
  • A combination of words and numbers can describe a path to move from one location to another. The order of the steps taken on this path is often important.

(time): How much ice cream can the cone hold? (capacity); Will my hand cover the cone when I hold on to it? (area); How high can the scoops be piled on? (height or length); I wonder how much heavier this ice cream cone would feel if I had a second scoop on it? (mass).

elaboration.value:
• identifying measurable attributes of an object:
  • measurable attributes of two-dimensional shapes:
    • length, height, width
    • angles
    • perimeter
    • area
  • measurable attributes of three-dimensional objects:
    • length, height, width, depth
    • angles
    • surface area
    • capacity
    • mass

content.name: Content
content.value: identify measurable attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects, including length, area, mass, capacity, and angle

content.name: Content
content.value: demonstrate an understanding of the value of Canadian currency

describer.name: Describer
describer.value: By the end of Grade 1, students will:

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• Every shape or object has several attributes that can be compared. The same shape or object can be described and compared using different attributes.
  • There are particular words that describe commonly measured attributes:
    • length is the distance from one point to the other and can be measured in any direction;
    • area is the amount of surface an object has;
    • mass is how heavy an object is;
    • capacity is the amount an object holds;
    • angle is the amount of turn between one line and another.

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value: Have students look at relevant real-life items and describe their measurable attributes. For example, give them a cup and an analog clock. They might notice that both objects have a mass; that the cup has capacity (can be filled), but the clock does not; or that they both have lengths, including height, width, and distance around. Students might also notice that the hands on the face of an analog clock form angles.

content.name: Content
content.value: compare several everyday objects and order them according to length, area, mass, and capacity

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• comparing objects:
    • directly comparing one object to another:
      • length: lining up one object beside another
      • area: laying one surface on top of another
      • mass: holding an object in each hand or using a pan balance
      • capacity: pouring the contents of one container into another
    • indirectly comparing two objects using a third object:
      • length: using string to compare the lengths of the two objects
      • area: using square tiles to cover the surfaces of the two objects
      • mass: using a balance to compare the mass of each object to a third object
      • capacity: pouring the contents of both containers into a third container, one at a time (emptying the third container in between)

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• Objects can be compared and ordered according to whether they have more or less of an attribute. Comparing the same objects by different attributes may produce different ordering.
  • There are specific words and phrases that help describe and compare attributes:
    • more, less, smaller, and bigger often only describe general comparisons unless a specific attribute is included (bigger area; smaller capacity);
    • tall, short, wide, narrow, long, and distance are all associated with length;
    • adding the suffix “-er” or “-est” typically creates a comparative term (e.g., heavier, lighter, heaviest, lightest).
  • Objects can be directly compared by matching, covering, or filling one object with the other to determine which has more length, mass, area, or capacity.
  • When a direct comparison cannot be easily made, a third object can serve as a “go-between” tool to make an indirect comparison. For example, a string can be used to compare the lengths of two objects that are not easily brought together, or a third container can be used to determine which of two containers holds more water. Indirect comparisons require using the transitivity principle and the conservation principle.

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• contexts for using a calendar:
    • recording special celebrations (e.g., personal or cultural events, holidays)
    • recording upcoming events (e.g., school assemblies, pizza day)
    • recording appointments (e.g., doctor, dentist, haircut)
    • tracking data (e.g., type of weather, temperatures)

content.name: Content
content.value: read the date on a calendar, and use a calendar to identify days, weeks, months, holidays, and seasons

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• Time is an abstract concept that cannot be seen or felt. The passing of time can be measured by counting things that repeat. The passing of a day, for example, is marked by the rising and setting of the Sun.
  • Calendars keep track of days, weeks, months, and years, as well as holidays and seasons.
  • There are other kinds of calendars, such as lunar, solar, agricultural, ecological, and personal calendars, that keep track of personal, social, and religious events.
  • Calendars enable people to communicate a date to others.

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value: Make a class calendar, and discuss as a class which key dates to include. Ensure that all students are encouraged to share personal and culturally relevant events from their diverse experiences and backgrounds. Depending on their suggestions, some dates may need to be indicated on the calendar as a range of days, specific weeks, or months.

content.name: Content
content.value: Students learn to recognize Canadian coins and bills and compare their values.

describer.name: Describer
describer.value: By the end of Grade 2, students will:

content.name: Content
content.value: identify the various Canadian coins up to 50¢ and coins and bills up to $50, and compare their values

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• common Canadian coins and bills:
    • nickel – worth 5¢; silver colour with a beaver on one side
    • dime – worth 10¢; silver colour with the Bluenose schooner on one side
    • quarter – worth 25¢; silver colour with a caribou on one side
    • loonie – worth $1; gold colour with a loon on one side
    • toonie – worth $2; silver and gold with a polar bear on one side
    • $5 bill – blue with a picture of the Canadarm on one side
    • $10 bill – purple with a picture of The Canadian, a train with service from Vancouver to Toronto, on one side. A more recent version of the $10 bill is a vertical note with Viola Desmond on one side and the Canadian Museum for Human Rights on the other.
    • $20 bill – green with a picture of the Canadian National Vimy Memorial on one side
    • $50 bill – red with a picture of the Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker Amundsen on one side
  • less-common Canadian coins:
    • 50¢ piece
    • silver dollar (limited use)
    • penny (no longer minted, though in “play money” it might be used to represent the concept and unit of 1¢)

Note

    • The size, shape, and texture of the coins differ (e.g., dime has ridges, and nickel has smooth sides).
    • The special edition coins may have different designs (e.g., Mythical Realms of the Haida Series, Chinese Zodiac).

elaboration.name: Elaboration
elaboration.value:
• Canadian coins and bills differ from one another in value and appearance (e.g., size, shape, colour, image, and/or texture).
  • Identifying the correspondence between the abstract concept of value and the concrete representation of coins and bills.

Note

  • The value of money can be an abstract concept because it is often represented by currency that is not concrete or accessible.  
  • Being able to identify Canadian currency by size, shape, colour, image, and/or texture allows for quick recognition of different denominations.
  • An understanding of unitizing is applied to identify the relationships between coins and their corresponding values.

TEXT ON SCREEN: Spiralling In Secondary Math.


Students file up the front steps of a large red brick high school. Inside, they move along the hallways in clusters. A student smiles as they grab an apple from a basket. Another closes their locker in the hall. In a math classroom, small groups of students stand at whiteboards on the walls. A student writes equations with a black marker as a classmate looks on.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Micah Black, Student.


Micah solves an equation on the whiteboard as two classmates observe.


MICAH: So, we're spiralling through the curriculum, we're doing lots of different topics a bit and then coming back to them later, so I find that helps us. Nothing in math you only use one subject, you always have multiple aspects coming together to solve a problem.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Al Overwijk, Math Teacher.


Al points at a problem on the board and engages two students who watch with curious wonder.


AL: It's this idea of instead of teaching the mathematics in blocked units we're going to give them an overview of the entire course and we're going to dig deeper as we go.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Mylène Therrien, Student.


Mylène stands with another student, and they listen to instructions as Al writes on the board. Al steps away and they discuss the problem before them.


MYLÈNE: Spiralling in the classroom is when we take a certain subject and we learn it and we go to a new subject and we spiral back to the original subject so we learn little bits over time and we end up coming back to the same key idea multiple times throughout the semester.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Lynn Pacarynuk, Department Head – Math.


LYNN: Spiralling means to me that we go through the curriculum multiple times, each time increasing the level of complexity and the number of connections that students are making. So, the first cycle is typically very introductory, it could be very concrete, it's meant to be very accessible to all students and make connections to their prior learning. The second cycle, now that the foundation has been laid, ideally includes more connections to some of that first learning and a richer array of tools that the students have at their disposal.


Lynn smiles and engages a student as they draw a graph on the whiteboard. Nearby, she watches a pair of classmates deliberate how to approach their solution. Other students stare at the board looking puzzled, while another couple write fervently. 


LYNN: And then, typically there are three cycles sometimes there are more, but in the last couple of cycles the expectation is that the students are bringing a range of the experiences from the first part of the course, so that they can then solve any kind of problem. We want things to be very open, less scaffolded, by the last cycles so that students are able to quite fluidly move between the different curriculum expectations, the different concepts and make connections between all of them.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Colin Woodside, Student.


COLIN: I think that spiralling is when we take all of the small concepts we've learned and kind of combine them together into bigger more important ideas and then that's the big things that we're learning in the course.


LYNN: The spirals change all the time actually. I've noticed in all of my classes, there are some topics that I can in advance think work well together. What happens is because my classroom is very student-centred, and the tasks that I give students are quite open, the spirals change because of where the conversation goes. So, if I design a task that I think is a measurement task, but the students see something that relates more to geometry, or they make a connection to another topic, then I like to honour their direction as much as possible. I don't think I've ever taught the same course the same way twice, so in terms of evaluations when we've got multiple expectations, we do evaluate by expectation so I have multiple expectations that are represented on my rubrics, and I have separate criteria that I use for each of the different expectations. Those criteria are generally taken from the achievement chart and the math process rubrics that we have. I think one of the really important parts about teaching through spiralling is to have a really strong foundation in the curriculum.


Al stands with a group of students at the whiteboard and points to part of an equation. A student’s eyes light up with understanding as another student begins to write.


AL: So, they'll see all the curriculum maybe three or four times, or maybe some ideas are seen six times. Kids that struggle early in the course, that's no big deal because they're going to get two, three, four, maybe five opportunities to show me each of the big ideas in the course. I think that's this idea of multiple opportunities for students to demonstrate their learning and the curriculum document says by the end of the course the students will. It's not at the end of the first unit or the end of the second unit and that's the only time they can show me that particular expectation. They have right to the end of the course to do it and we're giving them multiple opportunities to do that.


Students huddle around as Al demonstrates an exercise using a newspaper. The class disperse into groups and begin to write on the board. Al begins to engage the groups as they work.  


AL: One of the other nice features of spiralling is by the time we get to the third or fourth cycle, we're allowed to do these tasks that are super rich, that have endless possibilities for in terms of what curriculum they can bring into them and they can last up to a week long and it really allows the students to flourish in terms of their creativity, what questions they want to ask about the prompt, and what mathematics they want to bring into it and how deep they want to go with it. So, I really like this idea. By the time we get to the end of the course, the activities are less teacher scaffolded and they're really like this open problem that we really get to see the kids flourish and some of the stuff they come up with is above and beyond what I would have expected.


An unfocused image of the high school hallway.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Thank You. Ottawa-Carleton District School Board.


LOGO: The word Ontario beside a graphic of a white trillium on a teal background.

LYNN:  We want things to be very open less scaffolded by the end of the last cycles so that students are able to quite fluidly move between the different curriculum expectations, the different concepts and make connections between all of them.


MICAH: Nothing in math you only use one subject, you always have multiple aspects coming together to solve a problem.


MYLÈNE:  So, we learn little bits over time and we end up coming back to the same key idea multiple times throughout the semester and that really helps our understanding because we build on it rather than learning it all and sort of forgetting about it we get a chance to build on the same ideas and come back to them so it stays fresh in our minds.


A bearded teacher looks on as Laura and a classmate talk through their work. In another classroom, Mr. Overwijk speaks animatedly to a trio of students.


LAURA: But here like we go off into our groups onto the onto the whiteboards and go through all the different problems and just really explore it in a way that can be linked back to real life more and so you just really understand it on a more deeper level.

TEXT ON SCREEN: Tamsin Clunis, Student.


TAMSIN: I'm able to talk to people more freely in my math class this semester because Mr. Overwijk makes it a very welcoming friendly place. REBECCA: Well, since we're working in groups we kind of because I think when we work individually sometimes we think that we're the only one having trouble with what we're doing. And so, when we work in groups, we can kind of feel a little bit less alone. And also, since the teacher is circulating throughout the class. It seems like you see a lot more accessible since in a lot of other math classes I've been in the teacher kind of just sits at the desk and is doing their work. And we're doing our work. And so, to get up and go to the teacher. It's feels kind of a little bit scarier.


LAURA: I find that working with all different kinds of people in my class is really helpful because there's so many different viewpoints like I could think there is there's no way to solve this like we're kind of stumped and then someone else from my group will come in and be like, oh, what about this. And this. I never thought of that. And we can solve the problem. And there's just so many different perspectives and different methods of solving the problem that you can find in different people.


A student points to a table of numbers on a board as their two groupmates look on. In another class, three students sit at a pod of desks working with lengths of rope and measuring tapes.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Quinn Jeffery-Off, Student.


QUINN: So, we get given materials or a problem, and we get to work at our desks and it's you. We're learning how to represent things in different ways, whether it's like using an equation or a graph or an image or a table. And they're all really good just kind of ways for me to understand all these different concepts in a bunch of ways.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Sarah McKeague, Student.


Sarah and a Tamsin look at a sheet of newspaper on a desk. Later, Tamsin draws out an angle on a board as Sarah and a classmate chime in.


SARAH: Usually like if I have a problem and in class I don't know how to solve the question. I don't know how to do it. I'll usually ask what people in my group. And if we all don't know. We usually go to like another group and ask and then we'll ask Mr. Overwijk and he usually will give us a hint that will help us to figure it out.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Josh Franchuk, Student.


Josh and a peer discuss a problem. Josh turns and scans the other white boards. Later, Al stands at the front of the room speaking to the class.


JOSH: Well, when we get stuck which happens often enough, we go and we look at other whiteboards talk to other people. Worst case scenario, we'll ask Mr. Overwijk to come over here, and when we do need help, he doesn't necessarily tell us what to do. He'll just get our brains started and thinking in the direction of how we should be thinking to solve the problem. So, we end up on our own answering the question rather than just telling us.


Micah scribbles an algebraic equation on a board as two classmates watch.


MICAH: In math class, I think I'm not doing much different than I used to. I'm still learning all the stuff that you do. But it's been less of the teacher giving you a worksheet and saying, do this work your old formulas and do it. Go figure out the formulas for yourself and then use them. That helps me understand formulas a lot better where they come from. How to use them. And then it lets you apply them to problems, word problems and stuff like that, a lot easier.


Lynn listens as a student explains a line graph on a white board.  A student with an unsure expression is reassured by Lynn. Elsewhere, Lynn asks a group about their solution. At another white board, Lynn offers advice to Laura, who draws out a grid by hand.


LYNN: When I hear students talking to each other. I hear them talking in a very informal manner with each other about the mathematics and coming to terms with the vocabulary of the work that we're doing. Which is really helpful for me because they are learning to communicate with each other and being forced to start learning the language that they have to use because they have to make sense to make sense of it to each other.


LAURA:  What I expected coming into grade 9 math was a very strict environment. Much harder material. And that's not what I got at all. I was really confused at first. I thought, well, when are we going to start. But then I realized they're almost tricking us into learning like they would put a problem in front of me. And I'd be able to do it. And I was like, wait a minute. But we didn't actually learn anything because what I thought learning was before was just doing work on a textbook and then not doing it like the hands on things that we do now. And it's a lot more relaxed and thus a lot more effective I find.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Karem Abdullah, Student.


KAREM: I find I would like to be this kind of math teacher math teacher because I just feel like I'd be a really friendly teacher and like, I would love to make kids feel like they're safe with me. And like I can help them.


Along a wall of the classroom multiple groups work diligently at their boards. In another class, Al listens to Josh talk through a problem. Al makes notes on geometrical diagrams in front of them.


REBECCA: I really enjoy that in this class. We always work in groups because I think it gives you different perspectives. And you get to hear other people's way of thinking. So then you have multiple ways of approaching different problems. And I kind of like that. Also, our teacher has it where we kind of try to figure out new concepts before he introduces it to us so that when he does introduce it to us it kind of just solidifies what we figured out. And it kind of stays in our mind a little bit more since we had to work to figure out what he's teaching.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Steven Massey, Principal.


STEPHEN: Typically, I think when students are asked to sit for 75 minutes a day. We know that whoever is doing the talking is probably doing the learning. And if it's the teacher doing the talking and not the students. Then we have to ask ourselves, what's going through our students minds.


Mylène, Rebecca, Laura and Tamsin walk along a hallway, chatting. In a classroom, Tamsin takes photos of a whiteboard with her phone.


MYLÈNE: We don't have much of how much homework at all, to be honest, because we do a lot of it in the classroom for studying. I thought at the beginning that it would be tricky because we don't have notes. So, we take photos of the whiteboards a lot or we take our own note on the side. I thought it'd be hard for studying but to be honest, because we understand what we're doing in the classroom. We don't need to study much so that sounds cheesy, but at the end of the day, I get what I'm doing in class because I've worked on it with other people. And because it's been explained to me. And I've had the chance to explain it to other people to understand what I'm doing. So, for studying. I don't find it harder. I find it a lot easier, to be honest than other classrooms.


AL: I think that most students when they make their notes they're more meaningful when they do themselves and they tend to make notes of things they think they might forget.


Lynn stands at the front of a classroom, speaking to the students at their desks. Lynn points to some of the student work on a white board, discussing it. Later, Lynn helps a student at their desk. A bearded teacher leads Laura and a classmate through a fraction puzzle on a board. Laura nods to Lynn and begins working as Lynn walks away.


LYNN: I teach students at grade 9 level and grade 12 level. And so that whole process of students developing autonomy starts at grade 9 and we work with students to become aware of their own learning styles of their own strategies that work best for them. They learn how to ask the right questions. On top of all of the math vocabulary that they're learning and all of the curriculum related strategies that we are teaching them. But I want students by the end of grade 12 to be able to write an assessment or solve a problem. And know without having to ask me how that process went for them and be able to articulate to me their own next steps. They shouldn't need to wait for me as the teacher to tell them how to learn and what they need to know.


LAURA: The activities and questions that we do and are asked are more broad like they're not like a very strict word problem or something. It's like, here's a graph can you find all the different ways to read this and all the different data that's on this graph. And if you were to continue going like this, what would happen if you were to change something, you just get to explore it all over the place until you completely understand everything and is just so much more easy, and it just feels so great when you understand everything in your life. I know exactly what to do.


An unfocused image of the high school hallway.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Thank You. Ottawa-Carleton District School Board.

TEXT ON SCREEN: Rethinking Assessment and Evaluation In Secondary Math.


Students file up the front steps of a large red brick high school. Inside, they move along the hallways in clusters. A student smiles as they grab an apple from a basket. Another closes their locker in the hall. In a math classroom, small groups of students stand at whiteboards on the walls. A student writes equations with a black marker as a classmate looks on.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Lynn Pacarynuk, Department Head – Math.


LYNN: So, assessment and evaluation have changed quite a bit for me over the last few years.


Lynn engages with a student at their desk, then oversees two other students as they solve a problem together on the whiteboard. Another student talks and points at their work on the whiteboard as Lynn smiles and looks on.


LYNN: It used to mostly take the form of a written test that students had to do. I would say that tests haven't gone away in my class. But formative assessment has taken on by far a much greater role in my class. And by formative assessment, I mean opportunities for me to give students feedback on their learning, for students to reflect on their own learning, and for students to help each other with their learning.


TEXT ON SCREEN:  Mylène Therrien, Student.


Mylène looks focused and works with a classmate on a problem at the whiteboard.


MYLÈNE: So, we learn little bits over time, and we end up coming back to the same key idea multiple times throughout the semester. And that really helps our understanding because we build on it, rather than learning it all and sort of forgetting about it. We get a chance to build on the same ideas and come back to them, so it stays fresh in our minds.


A group of three students look enthused as they discuss a problem at the board. One student hands-off a marker before another begins to write down their solution.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Laura Taggart, Student.


LAURA: I think that the biggest change that has improved math for me this year is that it's just a really different way of learning. And it's a lot more simple, but also genius because you don't need to remember so many things, they just go right into your long term memory because it's tied to things that were already there.


Laura watches from her desk as Lynn holds a bundle of rope and presents the students with a hands-on exercise. Then, students move their desks into groups and stretch out the various lengths of rope. 


TEXT ON SCREEN: Tamsin Clunis, Student.


Tamsin gathers with three of her classmates around a cluster of desks. Nearby, other students sit before a deck of playing cards that have been matched by number.


TAMSIN: So, the day before our written test, we come into class and then we are again assigned to random groups with his card grouping method. And then he gives us a sheet of paper with all the questions. And we go up to our board and we write down all, we collaborate, we do the problems, we write down all the answers onto the board. Then he comes around, he takes a picture to look at later and evaluate us.


Tasmin’s teacher snaps a photo of a group’s answers on a whiteboard. Then, he talks and points at their solution as they look on.


TAMSIN: And then the next day, we have our written test. And so that is basically the same questions as we had on the whiteboard test. So, it's really good preparation to have that whiteboard tests, so that we know what we need to work on or we feel comfortable. And then we have that one night to improve for the written test.


MYLÈNE: For studying, I thought at the beginning that it would be tricky because we don't have notes. So, we take photos of the whiteboards a lot or we take our own notes on the side. So, I thought it would be hard for studying but to be honest, because we understand what we're doing in the classroom, we don't need to study much.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Al Overwijk, Math Teacher.


AL: You know, the curriculum document says by the end of the course, the students will. It's not the end of the first unit or the end of the second unit, and that's the only time they can show me that particular expectation. They have right to the end of the course to do it, and we're giving them multiple opportunities to do that.


Lynn sits with a student and talks with them one-on-one. They share a smile as they read over an evaluation rubric.


LYNN: So, in terms of evaluations, when we've got multiple expectations, we do evaluate by expectation. So, I have multiple expectations that are represented on my rubrics and I have separate criteria that I use for each of the different expectations. Those criteria are generally taken from the achievement chart and the math process rubrics that we have.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Karem Abdullah, Student.


KAREM: When I get a test back, we get feedback and marks. Well, sometimes not marks, sometimes it is. At the beginning it was, but now it isn't really, it's just more feedback. During the self-reflection is helpful to me because I'm marking myself, so I know how I'm actually doing it.


Karem works in a group with some classmates at the whiteboard. One student points as they read from a page, while another writes on the board.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Josh Franchuk, Student.


JOSH: This is preparing me for after high school because it's a different environment to learn in. And I think moving forward, we're not always going to be sitting down and learning. We're going to be moving around and talking to people. And it's a great thing to get started in high school, talking with people and learning in that aspect.


Josh is welcomed into a group of his peers as they work out a problem on the whiteboard. Nearby, Laura independently marks numbers down a column.


LAURA: What I thought learning was before was just doing work on a textbook and then not doing like the hands-on things that we do now. And it's a lot more relaxed and thus a lot more effective, I find.


Al engages with a group of students as they huddle around a desk and glance at the board.


TAMSIN: Teachers trying to use this new way of teaching should definitely go for it. I think that's really helpful and they should definitely try it out.


An unfocused image of the high school hallway.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Thank You. Ottawa-Carleton District School Board.

TEXT ON SCREEN: Connecting with Parents and Families In Secondary Math.


Students file up the front steps of a large red brick high school. Inside, they move along the hallways in clusters. A student smiles as they grab an apple from a basket. Another closes their locker in the hall. In a math classroom, small groups of students stand at whiteboards on the walls. A student writes equations with a black marker as a classmate looks on. In another classroom, students work together on a Geometry problem at a blackboard. Their instructor engages them and points to the board before a student begins writing with a focused stare. 


TEXT ON SCREEN: Steven Massey, Principal.


STEVEN: So, the conversations I have with parents are, you know this doesn't look like what my math classroom looked like that I remember. Help me understand why you're doing it this way. And they're really rich conversations because we have conversations about what do we want for our numerate students. We want them to be critical thinkers. We want them to have transferable skills. We want them to see patterns in the world around them. We want them to be able to estimate. We want them to be able to think deeply about complex problems and also look at problems from a different lens. And those rich conversations that we have with their parents, I think really move the conversation along.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Al Overwijk, Math Teacher.


AL: I think it's hard to argue with: I'm asking your son or daughter to come to my class to collaborate and communicate, defend their thinking, justify their thinking, problem solve, make connections.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Lynn Pacarynuk, Department Head – Math.


LYNN: I've heard a lot of positive feedback from parents. They are happy that their student’s transition to high school has been smooth. They are very happy that their child feels comfortable and safe in their math class. They really like that their child's self-confidence in math seems to be going up. They like hearing about math conversations at home, which they often haven't heard in the past.


STEVEN: And from a perspective of supporting students in their behavioural choices that they make, certainly in the thinking classroom, in our math classrooms, we are seeing less students disengaged and more students engaged in their learning, which I think makes it a more positive environment for teachers and for students. And that certainly is a jumping off point to have conversations with parents about the direction that we go in.


An unfocused image of the high school hallway.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Thank You. Ottawa-Carleton District School Board.

TEXT ON SCREEN: Leadership Reflections In Secondary Math.


Students file up the front steps of a large red brick high school. Inside, they move along the hallways in clusters. A student smiles as they grab an apple from a basket. Another closes their locker in the hall. In a math classroom, small groups of students stand at whiteboards on the walls. A student writes equations with a black marker as a classmate looks on.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Steven Massey. Principal.


STEVEN: I feel very privileged to work with such a dedicated group of colleagues. They push my thinking every single day. And when I'm working with students in the math classrooms or in other classrooms, students push my thinking every single day.


In a math classroom, instructors engage with students and help them understand formulas on the whiteboard. Then, students gather in a group at the whiteboard and watch closely as one student works out a solution with a marker.


STEVEN: I think that's a significant change in how our classrooms are set up, how our lessons are set up, and how we construct the learning environment for the students, rather than students now learning from the teacher or from the principal. We're all learning together. We're a learning institution. So, we learn just as much from our students as hopefully they learn from the educators and our job is more about facilitating the learning and setting the dynamics where students can collaborate with one another, can be critical thinkers, can be resilient, and can work together on really rich tasks.


Students stand next to each other at the whiteboard around the perimeter of the room and work together on math problems. Two other students sit together and talk as they stretch out a measuring tape. Another student smiles as she leads a group and explains a solution on the whiteboard. Then, students huddle around a desk and look focused as they rip and fold a newspaper.


STEVEN: When we think about things like The Thinking Classroom and the Vertical Non-Permanent Surfaces that you see in our classrooms, I think our teachers are really thinking about ways to get students engaged in their learning, to talk with one another, to collaborate, and to be critical thinkers. What we're seeing in our classrooms is the culmination of a lot of hard work in thinking deeply about the shifts in mathematics.


An instructor gives hints to a group of puzzled-looking students huddled around a problem on a chalkboard. Another instructor works one-on-one with a student as she shows her work on a whiteboard.


STEVEN: From a student behaviour perspective, I have noticed a significant change in the level of engagement in our students. Typically, I think when students are asked to sit for 75 minutes a day, we know that whoever is doing the talking is probably doing the learning. And if it's the teacher doing the talking and not the students, then we have to ask ourselves you know what's going through our students mind. And that's when I walk into a classroom and I see rows and desks and when I see students not talking with one another about math, I'll be honest with you, we tend to see higher discipline rates.

What I have observed in the Thinking Classroom is students talking about math, interacting with one another, joking with one another. Smiles. Laughs. Engagement. There's lots of conversations going on.


A student writes on the whiteboard as another looks on with a smile. Nearby, another group talk and point at a diagram as a student draws it on the board. Another student laughs as she writes an answer on a chalkboard.


STEVEN: The vision of the math department, I think as I said, is one of collaboration with some very dedicated staff that I think, at their core, want to learn how students learn, how they learn mathematics, and what motivates students. From a timetabling perspective, we spend a lot of time. We believe that a timetable is very important. Teachers need to have the opportunity to collaborate with one another. We think we're very mindful of how we set up a timetable, where teachers can share common spaces, co-teach, learn from one another. We get teachers from different departments who have a wondering about teaching practice or about students or about instructional strategies. So, you might have a French teacher and a math teacher and a science teacher. Administration are involved in those as well. We believe in principle as co-learner and just being vulnerable. You know, my background is in science, but how powerful it is when a principal and a French teacher and a math teacher and a science teacher are together, co-planning a lesson together. So, as administrators, we really in this school focus on professional learning and get teachers from different departments together to co-create a lesson.


An instructor watches as a student leads a small group through a problem. Another  teacher writes down an equation as two students watch intently. A different instructor points to the whiteboard and engages with some pupils.


STEVEN: When teachers come in there they're asking to implement a new idea. Embrace it. See what you can learn from it. There is learning in every different teacher move. It may not pan out the way that we thought. But that's the growth mindset stance is let's try something. Let's see what learning instructional strategy we can use in the classroom today. And let's see what we can learn from our students about how they respond.


An unfocused image of the high school hallway.


TEXT ON SCREEN: Thank You. Ottawa-Carleton District School Board.

system.name: G9 Math - Sample course plans - What is a course plan

title.name: Title
title.value: What is a course plan and why is it important?

content.name: Content
content.value:
A course plan outlines and organizes curriculum expectations. It is a living document that is revised as educators become increasingly aware of the abilities, strengths, needs and interests of their students. A thoughtfully developed course plan:

  • ensures that instruction is sequenced in a manner that aligns with research about learning mathematics;
  • allocates the appropriate time for concepts and skills so that students have multiple opportunities to focus on the overall expectations;
  • ensures that all specific expectations are addressed at least once within the course;
  • and recognizes that some expectations need to be revisited several times throughout the course.

Note: These sample course plans outline possible sequences of instruction for a course. There are many ways to structure an effective plan for learning.

• The process of mathematical modelling requires: understanding the problem; analysing the situation; creating a mathematical model; and analysing and assessing the model.

Note

  • A mathematical modelling task is different from a real-life application due to the cyclic nature of modelling, which involves examining a problem from outside mathematics, modelling it, and then checking the model against the real-life situation and adjusting as necessary.
  • The process of mathematical modelling should not be confused with using a "model" to represent or solve a problem that does not require the whole process.
  • Mathematical modelling tasks can be utilized in many ways and can support students with making connections among many mathematical concepts across the math strands and across other curricula.

Strand A
Learning related to Strand A: Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) Skills in Mathematics and the Mathematical Processes occurs in the context of learning related to the other strands. As educators develop lessons and plan learning activities, they should consider:
  • where there are opportunities to teach and reinforce social-emotional learning skills in order to help every student develop confidence, cope with challenges, think critically, and develop a positive identity as a math learner
  • how the mathematical processes can be highlighted so that students are actively engaged in applying these processes throughout the program
  • how instruction and the learning environment are designed to be culturally responsive and relevant


Examples
The examples laid out in the curriculum are intended to guide teachers in thinking about how the learning for each expectation might be positioned and demonstrated. In planning students’ learning experiences, it is important for teachers to ensure that learning experiences are culturally reflective of students’ lived realities in the community and in the world around them. It is also important to acknowledge and affirm the multiple ways of knowing and doing that students may bring to the classroom. 

Sample Tasks
The sample tasks laid out in the curriculum are intended to be illustrations only, and should be replaced or supplemented with tasks and learning contexts that are affirming of, relevant to, and reflective of students’ lives and backgrounds, and that provide students with the opportunity to learn about diverse cultures and communities in a respectful and informed way. Such opportunities may include the examination of social and economic justice concerns (e.g., racism, classism, sexism), health issues, environmental aspects, and so on, as appropriate.

content.name: Content
content.value:
Provide students with a real-life situation that they can relate to, such as determining the seating arrangement for guests at a class event to be held in the gym (e.g., ceremony, concert, assembly).

Have students brainstorm questions that need to be answered, such as how many chairs will be needed and how the chairs should be arranged. It is important to honour student voice and student questions, as well as to encourage students to listen to and consider the questions of their peers.

Analyse the situation with students by supporting them in making assumptions, such as that all the students in the class will invite at least one guest.

Have students think about what will remain the same, such as the number of students in the class, and think about what can vary, such as the number of guests that are invited.

Have students determine and gather the information needed to solve the problem. Students may say that they need to survey their classmates to figure out how many guests they would like to invite.

Have students identify possible representations, tools, technologies, or strategies that could be used to help create a model for the arrangement of the chairs. Some students may create a diagram or use cubes to show their arrangement. Others may arrange the chairs in rows or around a table. Some may even create a pattern with their arrangement.

Pose questions to students to support them in analysing their chair arrangement model. Some possible questions are:

  • Are all the exits in the gym accessible?
  • Is there space in the arrangement to allow ease of movement for someone who uses a wheelchair or if someone arrives with a stroller?
    • If the answer to any of these questions is no, have students adjust their models and reassess.

Have students share their models with the class and discuss the benefits of each of the models.

system.name: Math - Primary - A1 - Identification Management Emotions

content.name: Content
content.value:
Grade 1

As students explore the likelihood of events happening and use terms such as “impossible”, “possible”, and “certain” to describe this likelihood, they may reflect on and identify various emotions they are feeling. For example, if, in a real-life scenario, the likelihood of rain is certain, they may associate that with disappointment at having to alter their plans. On the other hand, they may feel relief that the plants will receive the water they need to grow. Students may articulate or discuss various strategies that they could use in different situations to help identify, validate, and manage their emotions. Strategies could include identifying alternative plans or approaches, developing and practising a script to express their frustration and efforts to address things over which they have less control, keeping track of the time, making a list, and focusing on things over which they have more control rather than on things over which they have less control. Educators can also seek opportunities to develop their own skills and identify safe and caring people and culturally relevant resources that can support students as they deal with emotions that might arise (e.g., parent or other trusted adults, Elders, Métis Senators, knowledge holders, knowledge keepers, or outreach workers).

Grade 2

As students represent and solve fair-share problems, they may identify emotions that they feel in various scenarios, including those beyond the classroom, when objects are divided in different ways. For example: “When my friend broke the cookie to share it, there was a big piece and a small piece. My friend took the big piece and that made me upset. It was not a fair share!” When teaching students about fair-share problems, there is also an opportunity for educators to make connections to diverse perspectives, talk about equity language, and use culturally relevant resources while raising awareness of emotions connected to bigger-picture “fair-share” problems – for example, those that may arise in social studies as students learn about people, the environment, and global communities.

Grade 3

As students create and execute code that represents a mathematical situation, they may reflect on and identify various emotions they may be feeling about whether the code will work, such as pride, confusion, annoyance, apprehension, or excitement. Educators can support students by validating their emotions, making connections between the mathematical concepts students are coding and relevant experiences in their lives. For example, educators can explain that coding can involve a form of experimenting that is similar to learning how to throw a basketball into a net. If at first you miss, you can change the angle of your throw or where you shoot from. You can try something different, and with each adjustment, you will learn something new about what you are doing until you arrive at something that works. Educators should be aware that, as students go through the process of figuring out what works, they may experience a range of emotions. Students might also experience emotions connected to events outside the learning but show their feelings through the learning experience. It is important for educators to be reflective, patient, empathetic, and thoughtful about why students might be experiencing these emotions.
